questions.question: What is the difference between props and state in React?
questions.title: Props Vs State
questions.direct_answer: Props are inputs passed FROM a parent — read-only, the component can't change them. State is data OWNED by the component — it changes via setState and triggers re-render. Props flow down; state lives where it's declared and can be lifted up if siblings need it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[Parent owns state] -->|props down| C1[Child A]
    P -->|props down| C2[Child B]
    C1 -->|callback up| P
    C2 -->|callback up| P
    P -->|setState| R[parent re-renders]
    R -->|new props| C1 & C2
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The unidirectional data flow (the architecture principle this question is really about): data flows down as props, events flow up as callbacks. A child never mutates its input; it calls a prop function and the parent decides what to do. This makes components predictable — a component with the same props renders the same output (pure), and any state change traces to exactly one owner.

Lifting state (the follow-up every interviewer asks): when two siblings need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent, pass it down as props, and pass setters/callbacks down for changes. The cost: intermediate components pass props they don't use (prop drilling) — the fix is composition (children as props), context for genuinely global data (theme, auth), or a state library (Zustand, Redux) when the tree gets deep.

State colocation (the design skill that separates seniors): keep state as close to where it's used as possible. Don't put everything in one top-level store by default — colocated state means fewer re-renders, simpler components, and less coupling. Lift only when sharing is required.
